places.title: Old Man of Storr
places.summary: Skye's best-known landmark: a 50 m pinnacle of rock below the Trotternish ridge, reached by a steep walk of about two hours there and back.
places.content:
The Old Man of Storr is the tallest of a group of rock pinnacles standing below the cliffs of the Storr, on the east side of the Trotternish peninsula. On a clear day it can be seen from far along the coast road, and from the sea beyond.

It is the work of an ancient landslip. The Trotternish ridge is an escarpment some 30 km (19 miles) long, where a heavy cap of volcanic rock sits on weaker sediments from the Jurassic period. Long ago the edge gave way and slid towards the sea, leaving the pinnacles behind. The ground is still not entirely at rest: in the summer of 2004 large rocks fell from the cliff and came to a stop at the foot of the Old Man.

In Gaelic it is Bodach an Stòir. One local story says the pinnacle is the thumb of a giant who lies buried in the hillside; another, that the cliff shows the face of an old man.

The walk starts at the car park beside the A855. The path is well made but steep and exposed to the weather, and it climbs steadily all the way. Most people go as far as the foot of the pinnacle and the viewpoint just above it, which looks back over the Old Man to the Sound of Raasay and the mainland. Beyond that point the ground is rougher and calls for a map, a compass and hill experience.
places.directions: 11 km (7 miles) north of Portree on the A855 towards Staffin, about 15 minutes by car. The car park is on the left; in summer it fills by mid-morning.
places.best_time: Before 9:00, ahead of the tour coaches, or late in the afternoon. Summer has the long light and the crowds.
tips: Wear boots or shoes with a good grip and carry a waterproof, even on a fine morning.
The main car park has a height barrier: motorhomes and tall vans use the marked bays on the road.
If the car park is full, come back later. Parking on the verges is not allowed.
The toilets by the car park are free. A kiosk across the road sells drinks and snacks in summer.
Phone signal comes and goes on the hill, so do not rely on it to find your way.

faq.question: Why is it called the Old Man of Storr?
faq.answer: The name is a translation of the Gaelic Bodach an Stòir. Local tradition explains it in two ways: the pinnacle is the thumb of a giant buried in the hillside, or the cliff behind it shows the face of an old man.

faq.question: How was the Old Man of Storr formed?
faq.answer: By a huge landslip. The Trotternish ridge is made of heavy volcanic rock lying on softer Jurassic sediments. The edge of the ridge collapsed and slid seawards, and the pinnacles are what was left standing. Rockfalls still happen: a large one came down in 2004.

faq.question: How much is parking at the Old Man of Storr?
faq.answer: £6 for up to six hours and £8 for up to twelve, the same for every vehicle. You can pay at the machines with cash or card, or with the RingGo app. Spaces cannot be booked in advance, and the main car park holds about 140 cars.

faq.question: Can you get to the Old Man of Storr by bus?
faq.answer: Yes. Stagecoach bus 57A leaves Somerled Square in Portree for Flodigarry and stops at the Old Man of Storr after about 15 minutes; the 57C brings you back. There is no 57A on Sundays, and timetables change, so check them before you set out.

faq.question: Are there toilets at the Old Man of Storr?
faq.answer: Yes, by the car park. They are free and include baby changing; the accessible toilet opens with a radar key. Beside them there is a free waste point for motorhomes.

faq.question: Can you park a motorhome or stay overnight at the Storr?
faq.answer: Motorhomes cannot enter the main car park because of the height barrier, but there are bays for them and other large vehicles on the road. Nobody may stay overnight: use one of the campsites nearby.

faq.question: What should you wear for the walk?
faq.answer: Footwear that supports the ankle and grips on wet rock, and layers with a waterproof on top. The path is steep and open to the wind, and the weather can turn within minutes. Take water, and sunscreen in summer.

faq.question: Is there an electric car charger?
faq.answer: Yes, the car park has both fast and standard chargers. In summer they are often in use, so have a second option in mind.

places.title: Quiraing
places.summary: The largest landslip in Britain, still moving: a viewpoint by the road and a 2-hour loop walk among pinnacles, with the Needle, the Table and the Prison.
places.content:
The Quiraing is the northern end of the great landslip that runs the length of the Trotternish ridge, and the most dramatic part of it. Below the cliffs of Meall na Suiramach the ground has broken into towers, ledges and hidden hollows, and it has not finished moving: the road at its foot has to be repaired again and again.

Three features have names. The Needle is a jagged pinnacle; the Prison is a block of rock that looks like a ruined keep; and the Table is a flat meadow raised among the cliffs, out of sight from below, where local tradition says cattle were hidden from raiders.

You do not have to walk far. The view from the car park, at the top of the pass between Staffin and Uig, already takes in the whole sweep of cliffs and the sea beyond, and the first kilometre of the path is close to level. The full circuit goes on below the crags and comes back over the top: about 6.8 km and two hours without stops, with narrow, exposed stretches that are slippery when wet.
places.directions: Single-track road between Staffin and Uig. Car park at the top of the pass, pay-and-display.
places.best_time: Morning light; often windy at the top.
tips: The first stretch of the path gives most of the views; the full loop has exposed sections.
Arrive early in July and August: the car park fills.
It is often windy at the top even when Staffin is calm. Take a layer.
Autumn is quieter and the colours are at their best.

faq.question: How long is the Quiraing walk?
faq.answer: The full loop is about 6.8 km and takes around two hours of walking, more with stops for photographs. It starts and ends at the car park. If you only have half an hour, go along the first, almost level stretch of the path and turn back: that part already has the classic views.

faq.question: Where do you park for the Quiraing?
faq.answer: At the car park on top of the pass, on the single-track road between Staffin and Uig. It is about 4 km from Staffin and 9 km from Uig, and around half an hour's drive from Portree. There is a charge, and in summer it fills early in the day.

faq.question: What are the Needle, the Table and the Prison?
faq.answer: They are the three best-known rock formations of the Quiraing. The Needle is a tall, sharp pinnacle. The Prison is a mass of rock that resembles a fortress. The Table is a flat grassy platform tucked in among the cliffs, which you only see once you have climbed up to it.

faq.question: Is the Quiraing still moving?
faq.answer: Yes. It is part of the Trotternish landslip, and this section still creeps downhill a little each year, which is why the road below needs regular repairs.

faq.question: Can you visit the Quiraing in bad weather?
faq.answer: You can see it from the car park in almost any weather, but the path is exposed, narrow in places and slippery after rain. In strong wind or thick cloud, stay near the start.

faq.question: Is the road to the Quiraing difficult to drive?
faq.answer: It is single-track with passing places. The climb from Staffin is steep with tight bends; the side that comes up from Uig is gentler. Large motorhomes do better approaching from Uig.

places.title: Kilt Rock and Mealt Falls
places.summary: A 55 m sea cliff of basalt columns that looks like a pleated kilt, with a waterfall dropping straight into the sea. A 10-minute roadside stop.
places.content:
Kilt Rock is a sea cliff about 55 m high on the east coast of Trotternish. Its upper part is made of vertical columns of dark basalt resting on bands of paler rock, and the pattern looks like the pleats of a kilt, which is where the name comes from.

Right beside the viewpoint, the water of Loch Mealt runs out over the edge of the cliff and drops straight into the sea. On a windy day the fall is blown back up in spray before it reaches the water.

This is a stop of a few minutes, not a walk: the railings are a few steps from the car park. Look down as well as along the cliff. Seabirds nest on the ledges, and dolphins and whales are sometimes seen offshore.
places.directions: On the A855 between Portree and Staffin; signposted lay-by with car park.
places.best_time: Any time; dramatic in wind and rain.
tips: Combine it with the dinosaur footprints at An Corran beach, at low tide.
After heavy rain the fall is at its best; in a strong wind, expect spray at the railings.
Lealt Falls is a short drive south and takes another fifteen minutes.

faq.question: Why is it called Kilt Rock?
faq.answer: Because of how the cliff looks. Columns of basalt run down it like pleats, over horizontal bands of lighter rock, and together they resemble the folds and pattern of a kilt.

faq.question: How high is the waterfall at Kilt Rock?
faq.answer: Mealt Falls drops about 55 m from the cliff top directly into the sea. It is fed by Loch Mealt, the small loch on the other side of the road.

faq.question: Is there a walk at Kilt Rock?
faq.answer: No. The viewpoint is a railed platform beside the car park, so it is a short stop suitable for everyone, including pushchairs and wheelchairs.

faq.question: Can you see dinosaur footprints near Kilt Rock?
faq.answer: Yes, a few minutes' drive north at An Corran beach in Staffin, where footprints are preserved in the rock on the shore. They are only visible at low tide and are easy to miss, so check the tide times.

places.title: Fairy Glen
places.summary: A miniature landscape of grassy cone hills, a tiny loch and a rock tower called Castle Ewen, near Uig. An easy 45-minute wander.
places.content:
The Fairy Glen is a small hollow in the hills above Uig that looks like the rest of Trotternish seen in miniature: grassy cones with ridged sides, a tiny loch, twisted rowan trees and, above them all, a tower of rock known as Castle Ewen. Like the Quiraing, it was shaped by a landslip, only on a much smaller scale.

Despite the name, there is no old legend attached to it. People began to call it the Fairy Glen simply because it looks like the kind of place where fairies would live.

It is a place to wander rather than to follow a route. Paths lead between the knolls and up to the foot of Castle Ewen, and a short scramble through a gap in the rock brings you out on top. The ground is grassy and uneven, and after rain it is muddy.
places.directions: Single-track road from Uig signposted Balnaknock/Sheader. Small car park; do not park on the verge.
places.best_time: Late afternoon light; avoid midday in summer.
tips: The access road is very narrow: not for motorhomes.
Wear waterproof footwear. The grass is boggy after rain.
Late afternoon has the best light and fewer people than midday.
In spring the slopes are covered in wildflowers.

faq.question: How do you get to the Fairy Glen?
faq.answer: From Uig. Just south of the village, a minor road signed for Sheader and Balnaknock leaves the main road and climbs inland; the glen is a couple of kilometres along it. The road is very narrow, so use the signed car park and walk the last part, and never park on the verges.

faq.question: Is the Fairy Glen the same as the Fairy Pools?
faq.answer: No. They are two different places on opposite sides of the island. The Fairy Glen is near Uig, in the north. The Fairy Pools are in Glen Brittle, in the south-west, about an hour and a half away by car.

faq.question: Why is it called the Fairy Glen?
faq.answer: Only because of its appearance. No traditional story links the place to fairies; the name is recent and comes from its odd, small-scale landscape.

faq.question: Can you climb Castle Ewen?
faq.answer: Yes. It is a short, steep scramble through a narrow cleft to a small flat top with a view over the glen. It is slippery when wet and there is a drop, so it is not for small children or anyone unsure on rock.

faq.question: Can you make stone circles in the Fairy Glen?
faq.answer: Please do not. Visitors used to arrange stones into spirals, and local people remove them: moving stones damages the ground and is not part of any tradition here. Leave the glen as you find it.

faq.question: When are the midges worst?
faq.answer: From June to August, in calm, damp weather, above all early and late in the day. Bring repellent in those months.

places.title: Fairy Pools
places.summary: Crystal-clear pools and small waterfalls on the River Brittle below the Black Cuillin. An easy 40-minute walk each way from the car park.
places.content:
The Fairy Pools are a chain of clear pools and small waterfalls on a mountain burn that comes down from the Black Cuillin into Glen Brittle. The water is cold, very clear and blue-green over pale rock, with the dark wall of the Cuillin behind.

A path leaves from opposite the car park and follows the burn uphill, crossing it on footbridges. The first large waterfall and pool are about 1.2 km from the start, so the walk there and back is 2.4 km; allow anything from forty minutes to an hour and a half, depending on how far up you go and how long you stay. The path is well made for most of the way, but one short stretch is steep and rocky, which rules out wheelchairs and pushchairs.

People do swim here. The water comes off the mountain and is very cold even in August, so it is a quick dip, not a swim.
places.directions: From the Carbost road, take the single-track road signed for Glenbrittle. The pay car park is on the right after about 8 km; the path starts across the road.
places.best_time: After rain for the falls; early morning to avoid crowds.
tips: Go early or late: by mid-morning in summer the car park is full.
One stretch of the path is steep and rocky. Wear proper shoes.
Midges are out in calm weather from May to September.
There is no café at the car park. Bring water and something to eat.

faq.question: How long is the walk to the Fairy Pools?
faq.answer: About 2.4 km there and back to the first main waterfall and pool. Most people take between forty minutes and an hour and a half in total. You can carry on further up the burn to smaller pools if you have time.

faq.question: Can you swim in the Fairy Pools?
faq.answer: Yes, and there is no charge, but the water is very cold all year. Go in slowly, do not jump from the rocks into water you have not checked, and bring something warm for afterwards.

faq.question: How much is parking at the Fairy Pools?
faq.answer: There is a charge for the car park, which pays for the path, the bridges and the toilets. The price has gone up in recent years and differs for cars and larger vehicles, so check the sign on arrival. You can pay by contactless card or cash.

faq.question: Are there toilets at the Fairy Pools?
faq.answer: Yes, in the car park. They are free to use and include an accessible toilet.

faq.question: Is the road to the Fairy Pools difficult?
faq.answer: It is single-track with passing places for the last several kilometres, and in July and August it is busy. Drive slowly and use the passing places to let others by. In winter it can be icy. Vehicles longer than 8 m are not allowed in the car park.

faq.question: When is the best time to go?
faq.answer: Early in the morning or in the evening, when the car park is quiet. The falls are fullest after rain; the pools are at their clearest after a dry spell.

places.title: Talisker Distillery
places.summary: Skye's oldest working distillery, on the shore of Loch Harport at Carbost. Tours and tastings most days; book ahead in summer.
places.content:
Talisker has been making whisky at Carbost, on the shore of Loch Harport, since 1830, which makes it the oldest working distillery on Skye. Its single malt is known for a smoky, peppery, slightly salty character that people connect with the sea air of this coast.

You can visit in two ways. Guided tours take you through the distillery itself, from the copper stills to the casks, and end with a tasting; there are shorter tastings without the tour, and longer, more expensive experiences for enthusiasts. Or you can simply come to the visitor building, which has a shop and a bar and does not need a ticket.

The distillery is not at Talisker Bay, in spite of the name. It stands in the village of Carbost; the bay is several kilometres further on, at the end of a minor road.
places.directions: In Carbost village on the B8009. Car park at the distillery.

opening_hours.hours: Open most days; hours change with the season. Check the official site

places.best_time: Book the tour in advance from May to September.
tips: Book the tour before anything else: it fixes the timetable of the day.
The distillery closes some experiences for maintenance for a few weeks in autumn. Check dates if you travel in October.
The Oyster Shed, up the hill, is a local favourite for seafood.

faq.question: Do you need to book a tour at Talisker?
faq.answer: It is strongly recommended, above all between May and September, when tours sell out days ahead. Book on the distillery's official site before you plan the rest of the day around it.

faq.question: Can you visit Talisker without taking a tour?
faq.answer: Yes. The visitor building, with its shop and bar, is usually open to anyone, though at busy times access may be limited.

faq.question: Can children visit Talisker Distillery?
faq.answer: Under-18s must be with an adult and are not served alcohol. Tours have a minimum age, which changes with the type of visit, so check it when you book.

faq.question: What can the driver do at the tasting?
faq.answer: Scotland's drink-drive limit is very low, so the driver should not drink at all. Ask at the start: distilleries normally give drivers their samples in small bottles to take away.

faq.question: Is the distillery at Talisker Bay?
faq.answer: No. The distillery is in Carbost, on Loch Harport. Talisker Bay, with its beach of dark and pale sand, is about 6 km further west along a minor road, plus a walk from where the road ends.

faq.question: How far is Talisker from Portree?
faq.answer: About 45 minutes by car. From Inverness, allow around three hours.

places.title: Dunvegan Castle and Gardens
places.summary: Seat of Clan MacLeod for 800 years, with the Fairy Flag, formal gardens and seal-watching boat trips from the castle jetty. Allow 2 hours.
places.content:
Dunvegan has been the home of the chiefs of Clan MacLeod for some eight hundred years, and it is usually described as the oldest continuously inhabited castle in Scotland. It stands on a rock above Loch Dunvegan, and what you see is the work of many centuries, from a medieval keep to Victorian battlements.

Inside are the clan's treasures. The most famous is the Fairy Flag, a fragile silk banner that, according to tradition, protects the MacLeods when it is unfurled in a moment of danger. Beside it are the Dunvegan Cup and Rory Mor's Horn, a drinking horn that each new chief is expected to drain of wine in a single draught.

The gardens are as much of a draw as the house. Laid out from the 18th century, they include a walled garden, a water garden with waterfalls and woodland walks down to the loch. From the jetty below the castle, small boats go out to the seals that live on the skerries of the loch.
places.directions: 1 km north of Dunvegan village on the A850. Free car park at the entrance.
tips: Go in the morning, before the coach groups arrive.
Seal trips cannot be booked ahead: ask at the jetty as soon as you arrive.
Allow time for the gardens. They take as long as the castle.
Overnight parking is not allowed in the car park.

faq.question: When is Dunvegan Castle open?
faq.answer: Every day from 1 April to 15 October, from 10:00 to 17:30, with last entry at 17:00. It is closed to individual visitors for the rest of the year.

faq.question: How do the seal trips at Dunvegan work?
faq.answer: They run from 1 April to 30 September, from the jetty below the castle, and last about 25 minutes. Places are given on the day in order of arrival, there is no advance booking, and trips depend on the weather and the sea. You need a castle or garden ticket, and the boat is paid separately: in the last listing we checked, £14.50 for adults and £10.50 for children.

faq.question: Do you need to book tickets for Dunvegan Castle?
faq.answer: No. You can buy your ticket at the ticket office when you arrive.

faq.question: What is the Fairy Flag?
faq.answer: A very old silk banner, the most precious possession of Clan MacLeod. One story says it was a gift from a fairy to a MacLeod chief; another, that it was brought back from the East. Tradition holds that it will save the clan three times when raised in battle, and that it has already been used twice.

faq.question: Can you take a dog to Dunvegan Castle?
faq.answer: Dogs are welcome in the gardens on a lead, but not inside the castle.

faq.question: Can you see seals without taking the boat?
faq.answer: Sometimes, from the shore of the loch or the garden paths, but the boat is the reliable way: it goes right up to the rocks where they haul out.

places.title: Neist Point
places.summary: Skye's westernmost point: a lighthouse on a headland of sea cliffs, reached by a steep concrete path. The island's best sunset.
places.content:
Neist Point is the most westerly tip of Skye: a long, narrow headland of grass and basalt that runs out into the Minch, with a lighthouse at its end and sea cliffs on either side. On a clear day the Outer Hebrides lie along the horizon.

A concrete path leads down from the car park by a long flight of steps and then along the spine of the headland to the lighthouse, 2.2 km there and back. It takes about 45 minutes without stops, but everyone stops. Keep in mind that the easy part comes first: the return is a steady climb, with two steep pulls before the car park.

The lighthouse dates from the early 1900s. It has worked automatically since 1990 and its buildings are closed, so the walk is for the setting, not for a visit. The best-known photograph, with the whole headland and the light at its tip, is not taken from the path at all but from the cliff top to the right of the car park.

This is also one of the better places on Skye to watch the sea. Minke whales, dolphins and porpoises pass close inshore in summer, and gannets and other seabirds fish off the point.
places.directions: From Glendale follow the single-track road to its end; car park at the top of the cliffs.
places.best_time: Sunset; stay for the colours after the sun goes down.
tips: For the classic view of the headland, walk along the cliff top to the right of the car park before going down.
Very exposed: hold on to hats and children.
At sunset, bring a torch for the climb back.
There are no toilets or shops. The nearest are in Glendale and Dunvegan.

faq.question: How long is the walk to Neist Point lighthouse?
faq.answer: 2.2 km there and back, by the same path. Allow about 45 minutes of walking, and at least an hour and a half with time to look around. The way down is easy; the way back is all uphill.

faq.question: Can you go inside Neist Point lighthouse?
faq.answer: No. The light is automatic and the buildings are closed to the public. You can walk around the outside.

faq.question: Can you see whales at Neist Point?
faq.answer: With luck. Minke whales, dolphins and porpoises are seen from the headland, mostly in June and July and on calm days. Bring binoculars and be patient: nothing is guaranteed.

faq.question: When is the best time to visit Neist Point?
faq.answer: Sunset, when the low light falls on the cliffs. It is also the busiest time, and the small car park fills, so arrive early. Take a torch for the walk back up.

faq.question: Is the road to Neist Point difficult?
faq.answer: It is a long single-track road with few passing places, from Glendale to the end of the tarmac. Allow extra time, drive slowly and expect to reverse now and then. It is not advisable in a large motorhome.

faq.question: Is Neist Point suitable for children?
faq.answer: With care. The path is steep and the cliffs have no fences, and it is very exposed to the wind. Keep children close, and leave the pushchair in the car.

places.title: Portree
places.summary: Skye's capital and the practical base: the painted harbour, most of the island's restaurants and shops, and the departure point for wildlife boat trips.
places.content:
Portree is the capital of Skye and its only real town. It sits around a sheltered bay on the east coast, roughly in the middle of the island, which is why most visitors use it as their base: the roads to Trotternish, Dunvegan and the south all meet here, and so do the island's buses.

The picture everyone knows is Quay Street, the row of painted houses along the harbour, now shops, guesthouses and restaurants. Bank Street, one level up, is the main street. Fishing boats still work from the pier, and wildlife trips leave from it in season.

The name is usually explained as the King's Port, after a visit by James V of Scotland, who sailed to Skye in 1540 with a fleet to settle the quarrels of the MacLeods and the MacDonalds. Two centuries later the town saw another royal visitor: in 1746 Charles Edward Stuart, on the run after Culloden, said goodbye to Flora MacDonald at the inn that stood where the Royal Hotel is today.

Ships carrying emigrants to North America left from this harbour in the 18th century, when the island could no longer feed its people. In the 19th, steamers from Glasgow made Portree the commercial centre of Skye and brought its first tourists.

Two short walks start in the town. The Lump is the wooded headland above the harbour, with an old tower you can climb for the view of the bay and the Cuillin, and a natural arena where the Skye Highland Games are held in summer. The Scorrybreac circuit follows the shore from the north side of the bay round a headland and back over the hill; seals are sometimes seen from the path.
places.directions: On the A87, 55 km (34 miles) from the Skye Bridge. Car parks are signed in the centre, which is small and best seen on foot.
places.best_time: Early evening, when the day visitors have left and the light is on the harbour.
tips: In summer, book a table for dinner: the restaurants fill and there are not many of them.
Reserve accommodation months ahead for June to September. Broadford, near the bridge, is the usual alternative when Portree is full.
The supermarket and fuel here are the last before the north of the island.
Distances on Skye take longer than the map suggests: allow extra time for every drive.

faq.question: What does the name Portree mean?
faq.answer: It comes from the Gaelic Port Rìgh, usually translated as the King's Port. Tradition links it to James V of Scotland, who anchored here in 1540 on a voyage to bring the island clans to order.

faq.question: Is Portree a good base for visiting Skye?
faq.answer: Yes, and it is the one most people choose. It is in the middle of the island, it has the widest choice of places to sleep and eat, and the bus routes to Dunvegan, Uig, Staffin and Broadford all start here. The drawback is demand: in summer it is busy and rooms sell out early.

faq.question: How do you get to Portree without a car?
faq.answer: By coach. Long-distance services run to Portree from Glasgow, Edinburgh and Inverness. From Inverness the journey takes about three and a half hours, from Glasgow about six and a half, and from Edinburgh about seven and a half. You can also take the train from Inverness to Kyle of Lochalsh and continue by bus. There is no railway on Skye.

faq.question: How long is the drive to Portree?
faq.answer: About three hours from Inverness, five from Glasgow and five and a half from Edinburgh, without stops. The usual route is the A87 over the Skye Bridge.

faq.question: Where are the coloured houses of Portree?
faq.answer: On Quay Street, along the harbour. The best view of the whole row is from the road above, on the way up to Bank Street, or from the far side of the pier.

faq.question: What is there to do in Portree?
faq.answer: Walk the harbour, climb the Lump for the view over the bay, and do the Scorrybreac circuit, a short walk along the shore and back over the hill. In season, boat trips leave from the pier to look for sea eagles and seals. The Skye Highland Games are held here in summer.

faq.question: How far ahead should you book a room in Portree?
faq.answer: For the summer months, several months ahead. The island has far more visitors than beds between June and September, and Portree is the first place to fill.

places.title: Sligachan Old Bridge
places.summary: The three-arched 1810 bridge with the Black Cuillin behind: the most painted view on Skye, a 10-minute stop at the junction of the A87 and A863.
places.content:
Sligachan is a road junction, a hotel and an old stone bridge, and one of the great views of Skye. From the bridge you look straight up the glen between the two ranges of the Cuillin: the dark, jagged peaks of the Black Cuillin on one side and the smooth, rounded Red Cuillin on the other.

The old bridge, with its three arches, dates from the early 19th century and is now open only to walkers; the modern road crosses beside it. Near the car park stands a bronze of Norman Collie and John Mackenzie, the scientist and the local guide who together explored and mapped these mountains.

The river has its own legend. It is said that if you kneel on the bank and hold your face in the water for seven seconds, the fairies will grant you lasting beauty, provided you let it dry in the air without wiping it.
places.directions: At the Sligachan junction on the A87, 14 km south of Portree. Free car park by the hotel.
places.best_time: Clear mornings for the ridge; it is often in cloud.
tips: Clear mornings are best. The ridge is often in cloud later in the day.
The peaks above are for experienced hillwalkers only; the glen path is for everyone.
The hotel has a bar that serves food, and there is a campsite next to it.

faq.question: What is the legend of the Sligachan river?
faq.answer: The story tells of a warrior woman whose beauty was restored by the fairies in these waters. Ever since, it is said, anyone who dips their face in the river for seven seconds, and lets it dry on its own, will be granted eternal beauty.

faq.question: What mountains can you see from Sligachan?
faq.answer: The Cuillin. To the south-west are the Black Cuillin, with the sharp peak of Sgùrr nan Gillean nearest; to the south-east, the rounded Red Cuillin, with Glamaig closest to the road.

faq.question: Is Sligachan worth a stop?
faq.answer: Yes, and it costs nothing: the bridge is beside the main road between the Skye Bridge and Portree, and ten minutes is enough for the view. On a clear morning it is one of the finest on the island.

faq.question: Can you walk from Sligachan?
faq.answer: A level path runs up Glen Sligachan between the two ranges, and you can follow it for as long as you like before turning back. The routes onto the Cuillin themselves are serious mountain ground and need experience.

places.title: Kyleakin
places.summary: The first village on Skye, beside the bridge: a small harbour, the ruin of Castle Moil and views back to the mainland. A common overnight stop.
places.content:
Kyleakin was where the ferry from the mainland landed until the Skye Bridge opened in 1995. The bridge tolls were scrapped in 2004 and the village is now a quiet place just off the main road, with a harbour, a few places to eat and somewhere to sleep.

On the point beyond the harbour stands what is left of Castle Moil. Local legend gives it to a Norse princess, known as Saucy Mary, who is said to have stretched a chain across the narrows to charge passing ships a toll.
places.directions: Signposted off the A87 at the Skye end of the bridge. Free parking by the harbour.
places.best_time: Evening, when the light is on the castle ruin and the bridge.
tips: The path out to the castle ruin is rough and boggy, and the last part can be awkward at high tide.
Kyle of Lochalsh, across the bridge, has the nearest supermarket, fuel and railway station.

faq.question: Do you have to pay to cross the Skye Bridge?
faq.answer: No. The bridge opened in 1995 with a toll, but the charge was removed in 2004 and crossing has been free ever since.

faq.question: Is Kyleakin a good place to stay on Skye?
faq.answer: It is quiet and convenient for arriving and leaving, since it is right by the bridge, and it is where our three-day tour spends its nights. For exploring the island by car, Portree and Broadford are more central and have more places to eat.

faq.question: Where do the tours pick up in Kyleakin?
faq.answer: At the bus stop beside the Kyleside car park. If you are staying across the bridge, the pick-up in Kyle of Lochalsh is at the junction of Ferry Road and Kyle Prospect Road.

faq.question: Can you visit Castle Moil?
faq.answer: Yes, at any time and free of charge. A path leads round the harbour to the ruin in about fifteen minutes. It is rough and wet underfoot, and the last part is easier when the tide is out.

places.title: Lealt Falls
places.summary: A waterfall dropping into a deep gorge beside the Trotternish road, seen from a viewing platform a few minutes from the car park.
places.content:
The Lealt river falls in two stages into a narrow gorge on its way to the sea. A short surfaced path leads from the car park to a platform over the upper fall, with a view along the coast and across to the mainland.

A rougher path continues to the cliff edge above the shore, where the ruins of an old diatomite works can be seen below.
places.directions: Beside the A855 between the Old Man of Storr and Kilt Rock. Signed car park on the seaward side of the road.
places.best_time: After rain, when the falls are full.
tips: Keep back from the unfenced edges beyond the platform.
Easy to combine with Kilt Rock, a short drive further north.

faq.question: How long is the walk to Lealt Falls?
faq.answer: A few minutes. A surfaced path leads from the car park to a viewing platform over the upper fall. The rougher path that carries on towards the cliff edge adds another ten or fifteen minutes.

faq.question: What are the ruins on the shore below Lealt Falls?
faq.answer: They belong to an old works that processed diatomite, a chalky mineral once dug from a loch inland and brought down to the coast to be dried and shipped out.

places.title: Eilean Donan Castle
places.summary: Scotland's most photographed castle, on a small island where three sea lochs meet, reached by a stone footbridge. On the main road to Skye.
places.content:
Eilean Donan stands on a small tidal island at the point where three sea lochs meet: Loch Duich, Loch Long and Loch Alsh. A stone bridge of three arches joins it to the shore beside the main road to Skye, which is why almost everyone on the way to the island stops here.

The island takes its name from Donan, an Irish missionary who is said to have settled here in the 6th century. The first castle was built in the early 13th century, in the reign of Alexander II, to hold this coast against Norse raiders. For most of the centuries that followed it belonged to the Mackenzies of Kintail, with the MacRaes as its keepers.

Its end came in 1719. A Jacobite rising that year had Spanish backing, and a garrison of Spanish soldiers was left in the castle with the powder store. Royal Navy ships sailed up the loch, bombarded the walls, took the garrison prisoner and blew up what remained. A few weeks later the rising was defeated at the Battle of Glen Shiel, a short way up the glen.

The ruin lay open to the weather for nearly two hundred years. Lieutenant-Colonel John MacRae-Gilstrap acquired it and rebuilt it between 1912 and 1932, working from the surviving ground plan; the bridge dates from the same works. What you visit is therefore a 20th-century castle on medieval foundations, and it now belongs to a charitable trust that looks after it and keeps it open.

Inside, the rooms are furnished as a Highland home of the 17th and 18th centuries, with a banqueting hall and an exhibition on the castle's history. Some rooms are private. The castle has also had a long career on screen, as the clan home in Highlander and as an MI6 base in The World Is Not Enough.
places.directions: At Dornie on the A87, 13 km (8 miles) east of Kyle of Lochalsh and the Skye Bridge. Car park at the visitor centre, beside the road.
places.best_time: First thing or after 16:00 in summer. The outside is floodlit after dark.
tips: Tickets are sold only at the castle on the day: there is no online booking.
Last admission is one hour before closing.
Rucksacks and large bags are not allowed inside. There are free lockers by the visitor centre.
The classic photograph is taken from the shore by the car park, and it is free.
At high tide the castle is ringed by water, which makes the better picture.

faq.question: How much does it cost to visit Eilean Donan Castle?
faq.answer: In the 2026 season an adult ticket is £13. Visitors aged 60 or over pay £12, children from 5 to 15 pay £6.50 and under-fives go free. A family ticket for two adults and three children is £38. Tickets are bought at the castle on the day; they are not sold online.

faq.question: When is Eilean Donan Castle open?
faq.answer: Every day from the start of February to 22 December, apart from a few closed days in November and December. Hours are longest in summer, 9:00 to 18:00, and shortest in winter, 10:00 to 16:00. The castle is closed for the whole of January. The dates shift a little each year, so check the official site before you travel.

faq.question: Can you see Eilean Donan Castle without paying?
faq.answer: Yes. The famous view of the castle and its bridge is from the shore next to the car park, which is open to everyone. You only need a ticket to cross the bridge and go inside.

faq.question: How far is Eilean Donan Castle from the Isle of Skye?
faq.answer: About 13 km (8 miles) from Kyle of Lochalsh, where the bridge to Skye begins: ten to fifteen minutes by car.

faq.question: Is Eilean Donan a real medieval castle?
faq.answer: The site is medieval, but the building is not. The original castle, begun in the 13th century, was blown up in 1719 and stood in ruins for almost two hundred years. It was rebuilt between 1912 and 1932 on the old ground plan.

faq.question: Why were there Spanish soldiers at Eilean Donan?
faq.answer: Spain supported the Jacobite rising of 1719 and sent troops to Scotland. Some of them were left to guard the castle, which was being used as a store for gunpowder. Royal Navy ships attacked it, captured the garrison and destroyed the castle with its own powder.

faq.question: Which films were shot at Eilean Donan Castle?
faq.answer: The best known are Highlander (1986), where it is the home of the MacLeod clan, and the James Bond film The World Is Not Enough (1999), where it appears as an MI6 headquarters. It has also been used in many advertisements.

faq.question: Can you take bags into the castle?
faq.answer: Small bags only. Rucksacks and large bags have to be left in your car or in the free lockers beside the visitor centre.

places.title: Loch Ness and Urquhart Castle
places.summary: The ruin of one of Scotland's largest castles on a headland above Loch Ness, with a visitor centre and boat trips on the loch from nearby.
places.content:
Loch Ness runs for about 37 km along the Great Glen and is more than 200 m deep, which is why it holds more water than any other loch in Scotland, and why the story of its monster has lasted. The modern legend dates from the 1930s, when a new road opened up the shore and the first reports reached the newspapers.

Urquhart Castle, on a rocky headland about halfway along the north shore, is the best place to take in the loch. It was once one of the largest castles in Scotland, and it changed hands again and again between Scots and English in the Wars of Independence. Its end was deliberate: the last government garrison blew it up on leaving, during the Jacobite risings, so that nobody else could use it.

What remains is a wide ruin of walls and towers running down to the water. The Grant Tower, rebuilt in the 16th century, can still be climbed for the view along the loch. The visitor centre, set into the hillside above, has a film, a display of objects found on the site and a café with a terrace.
places.directions: Off the A82 on the north-west shore of Loch Ness, about 3 km from Drumnadrochit. Parking at the visitor centre must be booked online.
places.best_time: Late afternoon and evening in summer, after the coach groups have gone.
tips: Book both the ticket and the parking online before you go.
The castle and the loch cruise are separate tickets.
From April to August the castle stays open into the evening, when the coach groups have gone.

faq.question: When is Urquhart Castle open?
faq.answer: All year, every day from 9:30. It closes at 20:15 from April to August, 18:00 in September, 17:00 in October and 16:30 from November to March. Last entry is one hour before closing, and it is closed on 25 and 26 December.

faq.question: Do you need to book Urquhart Castle in advance?
faq.answer: It is the safest and cheapest way: tickets are sold for a set date and time, and they cost less online than at the gate. If you come by car you must also book your parking online.

faq.question: Can you see the Loch Ness Monster from Urquhart Castle?
faq.answer: People have been looking since the 1930s and nobody has proved anything, but the castle is where many of the reported sightings were made, and it has the widest view of the loch. Look out for boat wakes and floating logs, which explain most of them.

faq.question: Is the loch cruise included in the castle ticket?
faq.answer: No. The castle and the boat trips on the loch are run separately and each has its own ticket. Some cruises land at the castle, in which case entry may be part of the package: check what you are buying.

faq.question: Why is Urquhart Castle in ruins?
faq.answer: It was destroyed on purpose. The government soldiers stationed there in the Jacobite period blew up the gatehouse when they left, to stop the castle falling into enemy hands, and it was never repaired.

faq.question: How far is Urquhart Castle from Inverness?
faq.answer: About 27 km along the A82, half an hour by car. The castle is roughly 3 km from the village of Drumnadrochit.

places.title: Inverness
places.summary: The capital of the Highlands, on the River Ness: a compact centre with the riverside, the Victorian Market and plenty of places for lunch.
places.content:
Inverness is the only city in the Highlands and the natural stop between Skye and the south. It grew up where the River Ness reaches the sea, a few kilometres from the northern end of Loch Ness, and it has been the meeting point of the roads through the Highlands for a very long time.

The centre is small enough to see on foot in an hour. The castle stands on a hill above the river; the present building dates from 1847, though there have been fortresses here since the Middle Ages. Below it, footbridges cross the Ness to the cathedral of St Andrew, built of red stone in the 19th century. The Old High Church, on the east bank, has a medieval tower that is the oldest building in the city.

If you have longer, follow the river upstream to the Ness Islands, a string of wooded islets linked by Victorian footbridges that have been a public park since the 1840s.

Two places just outside the city explain a great deal of Highland history. Culloden, where the last Jacobite army was destroyed in 1746, is a short drive east; and Fort George, the huge artillery fort built afterwards to keep the Highlands down, stands on the coast beyond it and is still an army base.
places.directions: Where the A9, A82 and A96 meet. Several pay car parks in the centre.
tips: The last large supermarkets and outdoor shops before the west coast are here.
The riverside walk to the Ness Islands takes about an hour there and back.

faq.question: What can you see in Inverness in an hour?
faq.answer: Walk from the centre down to the river, cross one of the footbridges for the view back to the castle, and return along the other bank past the cathedral. If you have time left, the covered Victorian Market is a few minutes away.

faq.question: Is Inverness on Loch Ness?
faq.answer: Not quite. The city stands on the River Ness, which flows out of the loch. The northern end of Loch Ness is a few kilometres south-west of the city, and Urquhart Castle, the usual place to see it, is about half an hour away.

faq.question: How far is Inverness from the Isle of Skye?
faq.answer: About three hours by car to Portree, and three and a half by coach. The road passes Loch Ness and Eilean Donan Castle on the way.

faq.question: Is Culloden near Inverness?
faq.answer: Yes, the battlefield is a short drive east of the city. It was here, in 1746, that the army of Charles Edward Stuart was defeated, which ended the Jacobite cause and brought harsh laws against Highland dress and customs.

faq.question: Why is Inverness called the capital of the Highlands?
faq.answer: Because it is the region's only city and its centre for transport, shopping and administration. Roads and railways from the north, the west and the south all meet here.

places.title: Pitlochry
places.summary: A Victorian resort town in the Perthshire hills, just off the A9: one main street of shops and cafés, and a dam with a fish ladder by the river.
places.content:
Pitlochry grew up as a holiday town after the railway arrived in the 19th century and still looks the part, with stone villas and a long main street. It is the usual place to break the drive between Inverness and Edinburgh.

Ten minutes' walk from the centre, the dam on the River Tummel has a fish ladder where salmon can sometimes be seen making their way upstream.
places.directions: Signposted from the A9, about 45 km north of Perth. Pay car parks behind the main street.
tips: Salmon run the fish ladder mainly from spring to autumn; there is no guarantee of seeing one.

faq.question: When can you see salmon at the Pitlochry fish ladder?
faq.answer: Mostly between spring and autumn, when the fish are moving upriver to spawn. The ladder is a chain of pools that lets them get past the dam. Sightings depend on the season and the day, and are never guaranteed.

faq.question: Why do tours stop in Pitlochry?
faq.answer: It is the natural place to break the long drive on the A9 between Inverness and Edinburgh: a compact town just off the road, with cafés, shops and toilets close together.

places.title: Glencoe
places.summary: Scotland's most famous glen: a deep valley between steep mountains, crossed by the main road, with a dark place in Highland history.
places.content:
The road from the south crosses the empty expanse of Rannoch Moor and then drops into Glencoe between walls of rock. The mountain that guards the entrance, a steep pyramid standing alone at the head of the glen, is Buachaille Etive Mòr, one of the most photographed in Scotland.

Further down, on the south side, are the Three Sisters: three great buttresses, Beinn Fhada, Gearr Aonach and Aonach Dubh, that are in fact the ends of ridges running down from Bidean nam Bian, the highest mountain in this part of the country. The classic view of them is from the lay-bys beside the road.

Glencoe is also remembered for what happened in February 1692. Soldiers of the government had been living for nearly two weeks as guests in the houses of the MacDonalds of Glencoe. Early on the morning of the 13th, on orders from above, they turned on their hosts and killed some thirty-eight of them; others died in the snow as they fled. It was the breach of hospitality, more than the number of dead, that made the massacre notorious.

The scenery has been used in many films. Several scenes of the Harry Potter series were shot here, and so was part of the James Bond film Skyfall. A visitor centre near Glencoe village tells the story of the glen and its people.
places.directions: On the A82 between Tyndrum and Fort William. Lay-by car parks along the glen; the Three Sisters viewpoint is signed.
places.best_time: Early or late; the lay-bys are crowded in the middle of the day.
tips: The lay-bys are small and busy: do not stop on the road itself.
Weather changes fast here; the tops are often in cloud.

faq.question: What happened in the Glencoe massacre?
faq.answer: On 13 February 1692, government soldiers who had been lodged for twelve days with the MacDonalds of Glencoe attacked the families who were sheltering them. About thirty-eight people were killed and more died of cold after escaping into the hills. The chief had been late in swearing loyalty to the king, and the killing was meant as an example.

faq.question: What are the Three Sisters of Glencoe?
faq.answer: Three steep ridges on the south side of the glen: Beinn Fhada, Gearr Aonach and Aonach Dubh. They are the northern spurs of Bidean nam Bian. The signed viewpoint beside the main road looks straight at them.

faq.question: Where can you stop in Glencoe?
faq.answer: There are lay-by car parks along the main road through the glen, the best known at the Three Sisters viewpoint. They are small and fill up in the middle of the day, so do not count on a space, and never stop on the road itself.

faq.question: Which films were shot in Glencoe?
faq.answer: Several of the Harry Potter films used the glen for outdoor scenes, including the setting of Hagrid's hut, and the Bond film Skyfall was filmed on the road down nearby Glen Etive.

faq.question: Is there a short walk in Glencoe?
faq.answer: The best known is the path into the Lost Valley, a hidden hollow between two of the Three Sisters. It takes two to three hours there and back and is rough, with a river crossing and some easy scrambling: it needs proper footwear and dry weather.

places.title: Glenfinnan Viaduct and Monument
places.summary: The curving railway viaduct known from the films, and the monument at the head of Loch Shiel where the 1745 Jacobite rising began.
places.content:
Two monuments stand a few hundred metres apart at the head of Loch Shiel. The older is the Glenfinnan Monument, a stone tower with a Highlander on top, raised in 1815 on the spot where Prince Charles Edward Stuart rallied the clans in August 1745 and began the last Jacobite rising.

The other is the railway viaduct, which carries the West Highland Line across the glen on 21 arches in a wide curve. When it was finished in 1901 it was one of the first large structures anywhere to be built of concrete. It was already well known to railway enthusiasts before the Harry Potter films made it famous around the world as the bridge crossed by the Hogwarts Express.

A path from the car park leads up the glen and under the arches to a viewpoint on the hillside, about fifteen to twenty minutes away. From April to October a steam train, the Jacobite, crosses the viaduct on its way between Fort William and Mallaig, and that is what most visitors come to see. The days and times change every season, and the car park closes when it is full, so it pays to arrive well ahead.
places.directions: On the A830 between Fort William and Mallaig, about 27 km west of Fort William. Pay car parks at the visitor centre.
places.best_time: Arrive well before a steam train is due: the car parks fill.
tips: Arrive at least an hour before a steam train is due: the car park fills and then closes.
Steam train times change each season. Check them before planning the stop around a crossing.
The only public toilets are at the visitor centre.
Show a bus or train ticket at the café for a free hot drink.

faq.question: What time does the steam train cross the Glenfinnan Viaduct?
faq.answer: It depends on the day and the season. The Jacobite steam train runs from April to October, on dates that change each year, and usually crosses in the late morning and again in the afternoon. The exact times are posted at the visitor centre. In winter there is no steam, but ordinary trains still cross the viaduct several times a day.

faq.question: Where is the best place to see the viaduct?
faq.answer: From the hillside viewpoint reached by the signed path from the car park, about fifteen to twenty minutes on foot. It looks down on the whole curve of the arches with the loch behind. The path is uneven and muddy after rain.

faq.question: How much is parking at Glenfinnan?
faq.answer: The car park at the visitor centre costs £5 a day. Visiting the monument grounds is free. In summer the car park is closed whenever it is full, so come early, or arrive by bus or train.

faq.question: Which Harry Potter films show the Glenfinnan Viaduct?
faq.answer: It appears in several films of the series as the route of the Hogwarts Express, most memorably in the scene with the flying car in the second film.

faq.question: What does the Glenfinnan Monument commemorate?
faq.answer: The raising of the Jacobite standard on 19 August 1745, when Prince Charles Edward Stuart gathered the Highland clans here to begin his attempt to win back the throne for his family. The rising ended at Culloden the following year.

faq.question: Can you ride the steam train over the viaduct?
faq.answer: Yes: the Jacobite runs between Fort William and Mallaig and crosses the viaduct in both directions. Seats sell out months ahead in summer, so book early.

places.title: Fort William
places.summary: The main town of the west Highlands, on Loch Linnhe at the foot of Ben Nevis, the highest mountain in Britain. The usual lunch stop on the way to Skye.
places.content: Fort William is a working town rather than a pretty one, but it has what a long drive needs: a pedestrian high street with places to eat, supermarkets and fuel. Ben Nevis, at 1,345 m, rises directly behind it, though the summit is hidden from the town itself.
places.directions: On the A82. Pay car parks at both ends of the high street.
tips: The last big supermarkets before Skye are here.

faq.question: Can you see Ben Nevis from Fort William?
faq.answer: Not from the town centre: the mountain is hidden behind its own lower slopes. The best views are from further off, for example from the Commando Memorial near Spean Bridge, or from across the water at Corpach.

faq.question: How long does it take to climb Ben Nevis?
faq.answer: Seven to nine hours there and back by the main path, for a fit walker. It is a serious mountain: the summit is 1,345 m, often in cloud, and holds snow for much of the year. It is not something to fit into a stop on the way to Skye.

places.title: Loch Garry viewpoint
places.summary: A roadside viewpoint high above Loch Garry, known because from here the loch looks like a map of Scotland.
places.content: The road to Skye climbs steeply from the Great Glen, and near the top a lay-by looks down the length of Loch Garry. Seen from this angle, the shape of the loch and its wooded shores resembles the outline of Scotland.
places.directions: A signed lay-by on the A87, a few kilometres after it leaves the A82 at Invergarry.
tips: A short stop: the view is from the lay-by itself.

faq.question: Why do people say Loch Garry looks like Scotland?
faq.answer: Seen from this lay-by, looking west down the loch, its shores and wooded headlands form an outline very like a map of Scotland. It is a trick of the angle: from anywhere else the loch looks like any other.

places.title: Commando Memorial
places.summary: A bronze of three commandos looking towards Ben Nevis, on a hill above Spean Bridge, in memory of the soldiers who trained in these mountains.
places.content:
The memorial was unveiled in 1952 to the commandos of the Second World War, who trained at nearby Achnacarry. It stands on open ground with one of the widest views in Lochaber: Ben Nevis and Aonach Mòr to the south on a clear day.

Beside it is a small garden of remembrance.
places.directions: Beside the A82 about 2 km north-west of Spean Bridge, at the junction with the B8004. Free car park.
tips: It is a place of remembrance: families still leave tributes in the garden.

faq.question: Who does the Commando Memorial commemorate?
faq.answer: The men of the British commando units of the Second World War, who trained in these mountains from their base at nearby Achnacarry. The three bronze figures look out over the ground where they prepared for action.

faq.question: Which mountains can you see from the Commando Memorial?
faq.answer: On a clear day, Ben Nevis, the highest mountain in Britain, and its neighbour Aonach Mòr, to the south. It is one of the best roadside views of the Nevis range.

places.title: Five Sisters of Kintail
places.summary: A ridge of five pointed peaks rising straight from the head of Loch Duich: the mountain view of the drive between Skye and Loch Ness.
places.content:
The Five Sisters stand in a row along the north side of Glen Shiel, three of them above 914 m. The main road runs along their foot, and they are seen at their best looking back from the shore of Loch Duich.

The traverse of the whole ridge is a long and serious mountain day for experienced hillwalkers.
places.directions: On the A87 through Glen Shiel, between Shiel Bridge and Cluanie. Lay-bys along the road and beside Loch Duich.
tips: The tops are often in cloud; the view is best in clear weather after a front has passed.

faq.question: What is the legend of the Five Sisters of Kintail?
faq.answer: The tale says there were once seven sisters. Two were married to visiting brothers, who promised to send their own five brothers back for the others. The five sisters waited, and in the end were turned into mountains so that their beauty would last until the brothers came.

faq.question: Can you walk the Five Sisters of Kintail?
faq.answer: The traverse of the ridge is one of the classic mountain days in Scotland, but it is long and hard: eight to ten hours over rough, high ground, starting and finishing at different points on the road. It is for experienced hillwalkers in good weather.

places.title: Dunkeld
places.summary: A small Perthshire town on the River Tay, with a part-ruined cathedral on the riverbank and streets of restored 18th-century houses.
places.content: Dunkeld is a short step off the A9 and a calm place to stretch your legs. The cathedral, half ruin and half parish church, stands in lawns beside the Tay, and the old houses around the square have been carefully restored. The bridge over the river dates from 1809.
places.directions: Signposted from the A9, about 24 km north of Perth. Pay car park by the river.
tips: The Hermitage, a woodland walk to a waterfall, is a couple of kilometres away on the other side of the A9.

faq.question: What is there to see in Dunkeld?
faq.answer: The cathedral on the bank of the Tay, part ruin and part parish church, the square of restored 18th-century houses beside it, and the bridge over the river. All three are within a few minutes' walk of each other.

faq.question: How far is Dunkeld from Edinburgh?
faq.answer: About an hour and a quarter by car, up the motorway to Perth and then the A9.

places.title: Stirling
places.summary: The old gateway between Lowlands and Highlands, with its castle on a rock above the plain and the Wallace Monument on the hill opposite.
places.content:
For centuries Stirling was the key to Scotland. It stood at the lowest crossing of the River Forth, on the only easy way between the Lowlands and the Highlands, and whoever held its castle controlled the road north. That is why two of the decisive battles of Scottish history were fought within sight of the walls: Stirling Bridge in 1297, won by William Wallace, and Bannockburn in 1314, won by Robert the Bruce.

The castle sits on a volcanic crag above the old town. Much of what stands today was built by the Stewart kings in the 15th and 16th centuries, when this was a royal palace as much as a fortress, and the great hall and the royal apartments have been restored to how they looked then.

On the hill across the river is the Wallace Monument, a Victorian tower raised in memory of William Wallace. Both are plain to see from the motorway, which is how most people on the way to the Highlands first meet them.
places.directions: Beside the M9, about 60 km north-west of Edinburgh. The castle is at the top of the old town; its own car park is closed to most cars, so use the Castleview park and ride.
tips: Book online: it is cheaper than buying at the gate.
Seeing the castle properly takes at least two hours.
The castle car park is closed to most cars. Use the park and ride.

faq.question: How much does it cost to visit Stirling Castle?
faq.answer: An adult ticket is £18.50 booked online and £20.50 bought at the castle. Visitors aged 65 or over pay £15 online, and children from 7 to 15 pay £9. A guided tour is included in the price.

faq.question: When is Stirling Castle open?
faq.answer: Every day from 9:30. It closes at 18:00 from April to September and at 17:00 from October to March, and it is closed on 25 and 26 December.

faq.question: Can you park at Stirling Castle?
faq.answer: Not at present, unless you need accessible parking: the castle car park is closed to other cars. Use the Castleview park and ride, or walk up from the town; the castle is about 800 m uphill from the railway and bus stations.

faq.question: How long do you need at Stirling Castle?
faq.answer: At least two hours to see the palace, the great hall and the walls properly. From the road it is only a passing view.

faq.question: Can you take a dog into Stirling Castle?
faq.answer: No. Only assistance dogs are allowed.

places.title: Callander
places.summary: A small town at the edge of the Highlands, on the road north from Stirling, and a gateway to Loch Lomond and the Trossachs National Park.
places.content: Callander sits where the flat country ends and the hills begin. Its long main street has cafés, bakeries and shops, which makes it the first comfortable stop on the way north from Edinburgh or Glasgow.
places.directions: On the A84, about 25 km north-west of Stirling. Pay car parks off the main street.

faq.question: Why do tours stop in Callander?
faq.answer: It is the first town at the edge of the Highlands on the road north from Edinburgh and Glasgow, with cafés, bakeries and toilets along one main street: a comfortable place for the first break of the day.

places.title: Loch Lubnaig
places.summary: A narrow loch between steep wooded hills, right beside the road north of Callander: the first real Highland scenery of the journey.
places.content: The road follows the east shore of Loch Lubnaig for several kilometres, with Ben Ledi rising on the far side. Lochside car parks give a few minutes by the water.
places.directions: Beside the A84, a few kilometres north of Callander. Signed car parks on the shore.

faq.question: Can you stop at Loch Lubnaig?
faq.answer: Yes. There are signed car parks right on the shore beside the main road, a few kilometres north of Callander, with room to walk down to the water.
